section_summary: This section documents U.S. consideration of strategic exports to Japan, especially scrap iron and steel, aviation gasoline, petroleum technology, and metallic ores, as public pressure for an embargo intensified during June–August 1940. It includes corporate shipment reports, congressional and private correspondence, State Department replies concerning the Export Control Act, and detailed economic studies of Japan’s dependence on American scrap. Foreign Service reporting also examines Bolivian tin, Manchurian tin and tungsten facilities, suspected transit of metals to Germany, and scrap shipments from Colombia to Japan.

subfiles.title: Department reply returning Harry Ginsberg’s letter on scrap-metal shipments
subfiles.about: The Secretary of State acknowledges and returns Harry Ginsberg’s letter concerning scrap-metal shipments to countries at war.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that Ginsberg’s June 20 letter, forwarded by McCormack on June 26, received careful consideration. He thanks the representative for sending it and returns the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Phillips Petroleum report of May iso-octane deliveries to Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Phillips Petroleum reports commercial iso-octane supplied to Mitsui for export to Japan during May 1940.
subfiles.summary: Responding to the Division of Controls’ January request, the company reports delivery of 3,090 fifty-three-gallon drums of commercial iso-octane to Mitsui & Co. The shipment was intended for export to Japan.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Phillips Petroleum’s iso-octane report
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Division of Controls acknowledges Phillips Petroleum’s report of May iso-octane deliveries for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Phillips Petroleum for reporting its May deliveries to Mitsui for export to Japan. The OCR gives the quantity as 3,000 drums, differing slightly from the 3,090 drums stated in the incoming letter.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on aviation-gasoline production in Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a memorandum on aviation-gasoline production methods and American-built plants in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The referenced memorandum summarized methods of producing aviation gasoline in several countries and recent Japanese plants built by American concerns. It judged that Japan was unlikely to duplicate the plants without machinery from the United States and directs readers to file 800.6363/424.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch no. 4757 on Bolivian ore and Japanese smelting
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits a consular memorandum on Bolivian ore shipments and tin-smelting capacity in Japan and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: The covering despatch responds to the Department’s confidential instruction of April 18. Grew reports an estimated Japanese tin-smelting capacity of 4,000–5,000 metric tons annually and notes movements of metals and ores from the Americas through Japan and Vladivostok.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Bolivian ore shipments and smelting facilities
subfiles.about: Richardson assesses Japanese tin production, Bolivian ore purchases, and suspected transshipment of American metals toward Germany.
subfiles.summary: Consular reports describe mines and smelters at Akenobe, Ikuno, Osaka, Oita, and Ashio, along with a 500-ton Bolivian shipment nominally destined for Hsinking. British authorities questioned whether the shipment was actually intended for Germany through Siberia, while other American and South American metals reportedly moved toward Vladivostok. Richardson concludes that Japan produced about 2,000 metric tons of tin ore annually and had total smelting capacity between 4,000 and 5,000 tons.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japan’s Dependence on American Scrap
subfiles.about: The study analyzes Japan’s dependence on American scrap iron and its limited alternatives in pig iron and iron ore.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that the United States supplied roughly 89–90 percent of Japan’s imported scrap and that American scrap supported about one-third of Japanese steel output. It surveys export volumes, foreign controls, Japanese furnace practices, and possible replacement through pig iron or ore from Manchuria, Korea, British India, Malaya, Australia, the Philippines, and China. It concludes that other foreign markets could not replace two million tons of American scrap and that domestic substitution would require an impracticable fourfold increase in Japanese iron-ore production. The study also contends that conserving American scrap was becoming important for U.S. national defense.

subfiles.title: Geraldine Fitch letter urging an embargo on supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Fitch urges the administration to stop aviation gasoline, molybdenum, and other American materials from supporting Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: Drawing on reports from her husband’s relief work in China, Fitch describes the human effects of Japanese bombing and condemns continued American material support. She argues that high-octane gasoline is particularly important because Japan cannot readily produce it and asks for action under H.R. 9850. She rejects appeasement and requests a supportive gesture toward China on the July 7 anniversary of the war.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Geraldine Fitch
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Division of Controls acknowledges Fitch’s letter about American policy in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Allen thanks Fitch for communicating her views. He assures her that the Department will give them careful consideration but makes no policy commitment.

subfiles.title: Standard Oil report of hydro-polymer gasoline exports
subfiles.from: J. H. Tuttle, Standard Oil Company of California
subfiles.about: Standard Oil reports a May delivery of hydro-polymer gasoline for shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Tuttle reports delivery of 212,000 gallons of hydro-polymer gasoline, identified as iso-octane, for Japan. He states that it was the company’s first such delivery since the shipment reported on January 2.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Standard Oil’s gasoline report
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Standard Oil’s report of 212,000 gallons of gasoline delivered for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost records the reported May shipment and notes that it was the first since Standard Oil’s January report. He thanks the company for cooperating with the Department’s information request.

subfiles.title: Telephone memorandum on the Universal Oil Products lawsuit
subfiles.about: Moseley records Universal Oil Products’ request for government support in litigation over withheld gasoline-plant technology for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Healy asked what support the Department would provide against the Japan Gasoline Company’s suit over unfulfilled contracts for cracking and iso-octane plant information. He reported that company president Saneyoshi had arrived in New York and might involve the Japanese ambassador. Healy hoped the new defense legislation would convert the moral embargo into a legal restriction on plans and specifications, but Moseley could offer no assurance that such technical data would be controlled.

subfiles.title: A. Jandman inquiry about continuing scrap shipments
subfiles.from: A. Jandman, Perfection Carbon Paper Company
subfiles.about: The correspondent asks whether American scrap iron and other potential war materials are still being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Jandman refers to public discussion of shipments to Japan and directs the Department’s attention to an enclosed press item. The clipping mentioned in the letter is not present on this page.

subfiles.title: Senator Wiley’s transmittal of the O’Brien letter
subfiles.about: Wiley forwards a constituent’s inquiry about scrap iron and raw war materials shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The senator asks the Department to return J. F. O’Brien’s letter with a duplicate report that Wiley can use in replying. His transmittal frames the subject as American shipments of scrap and other war materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: J. F. O’Brien letter questioning aid to Japan
subfiles.about: O’Brien asks why the United States continues exporting war materials that Japan can use against China.
subfiles.summary: O’Brien says friends have questioned the apparent contradiction between American sympathy for China and continued shipments to Japan. He asks Senator Wiley for the correct explanation.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Senator Wiley on export controls
subfiles.about: Welles explains the legal status of exports to Japan after passage of the Export Control Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that no statute imposed a general embargo on commodities exported to Japan. It explains that the President’s July 2 proclamation listed materials to be prohibited or curtailed for national defense, but scrap iron was not then included. Decisions on additions rested with the Administrator of Export Control, and O’Brien’s letter was returned.

subfiles.title: Senator Brown transmittal and routing sheet
subfiles.about: The page represents Senator Brown’s transmittal of Helen Brower’s inquiry about scrap and gasoline exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Only the Senate Committee on Finance letterhead, roster, filing marks, and file number remain legible on this page. The Department’s subsequent reply identifies Brown’s July 12 communication as the cover letter for Mrs. Brower’s enclosure.

subfiles.title: Helen Brower letter on scrap iron and gasoline exports
subfiles.about: Brower asks whether anything has been done to control scrap-iron and gasoline shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Citing a Chicago Daily News report that Japan planned to double imports of American iron and steel scrap, Brower calls continued inaction folly. She asks Senator Brown about existing controls on scrap and gasoline exports.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Senator Brown
subfiles.about: Welles explains that scrap iron and gasoline were not yet included in the President’s export-control list.
subfiles.summary: The response repeats that there was no general statutory embargo on exports to Japan and summarizes the authority created by the July 2 Export Control Act. It notes that neither scrap iron nor gasoline appeared in the current proclamation and that recommendations for additions belonged to the Administrator of Export Control. Brower’s letter is returned with copies of the proclamation.

subfiles.title: E. B. Coolidge letter supporting export-control legislation
subfiles.about: Coolidge thanks Yost for information and endorses legislation controlling aid to Germany and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Coolidge assumes the information concerned Senate bill S. 2009 and describes it as important. He argues that American profit-seeking helped place Germany and Japan in a position to cause international suffering.

subfiles.title: Consular despatch no. 190 on Colombian scrap destined for Kobe
subfiles.from: Nelson R. Park, American Consulate, Barranquilla
subfiles.about: Park reports preparations to load roughly 3,000 tons of Colombian scrap iron onto the Yugoslav vessel BOR for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Railway cars carrying scrap were moving from Barranquilla to Puerto Colombia. Park learned that the cargo was destined for Kobe aboard the Yugoslav vessel BOR, expected from Puerto Rico on July 17. He promised further information when available.

subfiles.title: Roger Greene cover letter on Far Eastern policy
subfiles.about: Greene submits a memorandum proposing economic action toward Japan amid the crisis in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Greene warns that British concessions in Burma may worsen rather than relieve the situation. He says a just settlement in the Far East could simplify defense of the Americas and notes that copies went to senior executive and congressional officials.

subfiles.title: The Far Eastern Situation
subfiles.about: Greene proposes phased export controls, increased duties on Japanese goods, and financial aid to China.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies Japan, Germany, and Italy as potential opponents and argues that continued material aid increases the danger they present. Greene recommends licensing iron, steel, copper, scrap, petroleum products, and vehicles, beginning with an immediate scrap embargo and escalating restrictions if Japan remains hostile. He also proposes higher duties on Japanese luxury goods, especially silk, and liberal financial assistance to China.

subfiles.title: Department acknowledgment to Roger Greene
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Greene’s proposals for controlling exports and raising duties on Japanese imports.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that Greene’s letter and memorandum were carefully noted. It expresses appreciation for the spirit behind his submission without commenting on the proposed measures.

subfiles.title: Consular despatch no. 186 on a projected Colombian scrap shipment
subfiles.from: Nelson R. Park, American Consulate, Barranquilla
subfiles.about: Park reports preliminary intelligence about a planned 3,000-ton scrap-iron shipment from Colombia to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reported shipper was Adolfo Graubard, who allegedly bought the scrap from Julius Siefkin and Fritz Fuhrhop. A freighter believed to have been called BOR was expected at Puerto Colombia around July 18, and the Colombian government had reportedly issued an export permit. Park emphasized the urgency because the shipment would pass through the Panama Canal.

subfiles.title: Senator Overton request for scrap-export information
subfiles.about: Overton asks for the current policy and statistics on American scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: A constituent had claimed that the United States supplied 56 percent of Japan’s war material and suggested embargoes on scrap iron and high-octane gasoline. Overton expressly declines to endorse an embargo and asks only for information he can pass to the constituent.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Senator Overton
subfiles.about: Welles reports that iron and steel scrap had been placed under export-license control and supplies historical export figures.
subfiles.summary: The reply encloses the July 26 proclamation and regulations issued under the Export Control Act and states that licenses were now required for iron and steel scrap. It provides quantity and value figures for exports to Japan in 1937–1939 and early 1940, reporting approximately 350,000 long tons valued at $6.569 million for the stated 1940 period. License decisions were governed by directives from the Administrator of Export Control.

subfiles.title: Representative Wigglesworth transmittal of Florence Gurney’s letter
subfiles.about: Wigglesworth forwards a constituent’s protest against sending scrap iron to Japan and requests comment.
subfiles.summary: The representative encloses Florence Gurney’s letter concerning American policy on scrap-iron exports to Japan. He asks the Secretary for whatever comments the Department considers appropriate.

subfiles.title: Florence Gurney letter opposing scrap exports
subfiles.about: Gurney appeals for action to stop American scrap iron from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: She condemns exporters for supplying material that Japan can use against China and questions why war materials may be sold to a belligerent. Gurney contrasts these exports with American missionary, educational, hospital, and church work undertaken to aid the Chinese.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Representative Wigglesworth
subfiles.about: Welles explains the new licensing controls governing exports of iron and steel scrap.
subfiles.summary: The reply encloses the proclamations and regulations of July 2 and July 26 under the Export Control Act. It explains that iron and steel scrap may not be exported without a license and that the government can curtail or prohibit exports when national-defense needs require it.

subfiles.title: Representative Thomason transmittal of Howell material
subfiles.about: Thomason forwards an El Paso constituent’s letter and related material about exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The representative sends the communication for the Department’s information and possible use. He asks that it be returned for his files after it has served its purpose.

subfiles.title: Mexico Pipeline to Supply Japan With Crude Oil
subfiles.about: The clipping reports negotiations for a trans-Mexican oil pipeline intended largely to supply Japan.
subfiles.summary: The proposed line would cross the Isthmus of Tehuantepec from Puerto Mexico to Salina Cruz and carry about 40,000 barrels daily. Japanese Mitsui interests were reportedly prepared to purchase large quantities for military needs, while the Raymond Concrete Pipe Company of New York was associated with construction. The report says the project was encountering State Department objections to the American firm’s participation.

subfiles.title: A. L. Howell letter on an El Paso scrap shipment
subfiles.about: Howell reports that an El Paso dealer was rushing a trainload of scrap iron to Japan before an anticipated embargo.
subfiles.summary: Howell identifies the El Paso Iron & Metal Company and its owner, Isadore Feinberg, and demands immediate action against Japanese purchases of war materials. He argues that selling supplies to Japan contradicts American aid to China and predicts war with the United States. A postscript also alleges widespread Mexican sympathy for Hitler.

subfiles.title: Department reply to Representative Thomason
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Howell’s letter and clipping about oil and scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull says Howell’s comments have been noted and returns the constituent’s letter and clipping as requested. He also encloses the President’s July 26 proclamation and regulations under the Export Control Act.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Japanese dependence on scrap
subfiles.to: Henry F. Grady and Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: The memorandum highlights conclusions from Tokyo despatch no. 4788 concerning Japan’s dependence on American scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: It notes expected pressure on Japanese steelmaking from British demand for Indian pig iron and Malayan ore. Imported scrap represented an estimated 35 percent of Japanese consumption, with 80 percent of imports coming from the United States, and a stoppage was expected to reduce steel production by at least 15 percent. Japan was not expected to reduce this dependence appreciably before the end of 1941.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch no. 4788 transmitting a Japanese article on scrap imports
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits a translated excerpt showing the Japanese steel industry’s reliance on imported American scrap.
subfiles.summary: The embassy presents the article in connection with reports that the United States might restrict scrap exports. Grew describes the excerpt from the Tokyo economic journal Diamond as significant evidence of Japanese industrial dependence.

subfiles.title: Translated Diamond article on Japanese scrap-iron imports
subfiles.to: Department of State, as an embassy enclosure
subfiles.about: The article analyzes threats to Japan’s supplies of American scrap, Indian pig iron, and Malayan ore.
subfiles.summary: The article estimates that scrap consumption equaled roughly 70 percent of Japanese steel output and that imports supplied 35 percent of consumption, with the United States furnishing 80 percent of imported scrap. It warns that an American stoppage could cut steel production by at least 15 percent and that no other foreign source could supply equivalent quantities. Anticipating embargo pressure, increased American demand, and Allied purchases, it recommends conservation, more efficient blast-furnace operation, ore-refining facilities, and diplomatic efforts to secure scrap until Japan could reduce dependence after 1941.

subfiles.title: Embassy despatch no. 4790 on Manchurian tin and tungsten
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew forwards a Dairen consular report on Manchurian tin and tungsten facilities and possible metal shipments to Germany.
subfiles.summary: The despatch supplements the embassy’s earlier report no. 4757. Grew says the enclosed communication indicates that Manchurian plants for smelting tin ore and wolfram were being built or may have been completed. Although firm evidence was lacking, the report also found grounds to suspect that metals were beginning to move through Manchuria to Germany.

subfiles.title: Report on production and importation of tin and tungsten in Manchuria
subfiles.about: The report surveys Manchurian regulation, mining, refining, and trade in tin and tungsten and investigates possible transit shipments to Germany.
subfiles.summary: The report describes Manchukuo laws controlling tin and tungsten and notes fragmentary evidence of new tungsten mining, refining equipment, and limited experimental tin work near Dairen. It discusses possible plant locations at Fushun, Antung, Tasung, or Jilin and suggests consulting American adviser Ralph Vaill. A 500-ton Bolivian tin-ore shipment consigned to Hsinking remained unexplained, while additional lead, zinc spelter, antimony, and possibly copper shipments prompted suspicion that supplies nominally intended for Manchuria were being forwarded to Germany. The consul emphasizes that evidence remained incomplete and promises continued investigation.

subfiles.title: Consular report on the BOR loading scrap for Osaka
subfiles.from: Nelson R. Park, American Consulate, Barranquilla
subfiles.about: Park confirms the BOR’s arrival at Puerto Colombia to load a large cargo of scrap iron for Osaka.
subfiles.summary: The Yugoslav steamship BOR arrived from San Juan with about 3,100 tons of scrap already aboard and expected to load another 2,680 tons at Puerto Colombia. Its agent reported a net tonnage of 2,212, a crew of 32 under master R. Popovic, and a route to Osaka through the Panama Canal and Hawaii. Park encloses Vice Consul Phelan’s July 17 memorandum and reports an expected sailing for Cristóbal around July 22.
